## 1 - Dataset choice, collection and presentation

The dataset used for this project concerns financial data time series. All
the variables were individually collected from the Investing.com financial
data bank and appended into a dataframe. Six numerical variables have been
extracted from the daily time series data bank within a time range of four
years, from 01/01/2019 to 31/12/2022, for a total of 1019 observations for
each variable.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)

library(knitr)      # kable()
library(leaps)      # regsubsets()
library(car)        # vif(), residualPlots()
library(faraway)    # halfnorm()
library(effects)    # predictorEffects()
```

```{r load-data}
# --- SYNTHETIC DATA NOTICE ---
# The original raw CSV files behind `data_fin1` were never part of the
# source material for this migration (see reconstruction note above), and a
# like-for-like free daily series for all six original variables (FTSE
# Italia Banks index, BTP price, VSTOXX, BTP-Bund spread, EUR/USD, Italian
# 10Y CDS, 2019-2022) could not be reliably sourced without a paid data
# feed. To let the rest of this document actually run end-to-end, this
# chunk builds a clearly-labelled SYNTHETIC substitute dataset instead of a
# real one, with the same shape (1019 daily observations, 6 numeric
# columns) and realistic financial-series properties:
#   - each predictor is an AR(1)-smoothed (phi = 0.97) series, so it is
#     persistent/trending like a real daily financial series rather than iid;
#   - the five predictors are built from correlated innovations (via a
#     Cholesky factor of a target correlation matrix) so they reproduce the
#     same *qualitative* collinearity pattern described in the report
#     (BTP highly correlated with Spread and EUR, Spread/CDS highly
#     correlated, VIX comparatively uncorrelated with the others);
#   - the response (Banks) is generated from the five predictors (using
#     log(VIX), not VIX, as the true driver) plus autocorrelated noise
#     whose variance increases with VIX, so that `lm(Banks ~ .)` below (a
#     linear-in-VIX model) lands close to the original report's adjusted
#     R^2 (~0.66-0.70) with all five predictors significant, while also
#     genuinely exhibiting the non-linearity/non-constant-variance-in-VIX
#     pattern the report diagnoses in Section 7, and genuinely improving
#     (not just in the preserved historical text) once VIX is
#     log-transformed and high-leverage points/outliers are removed in
#     Section 8 - this is what makes the subset selection, diagnostics and
#     model-improvement sections meaningful to run rather than trivial or
#     degenerate.
# This is NOT real market data and none of the resulting numbers should be
# read as a restatement of the original project's findings. See the README
# ("Dataset" section) for the full rationale.
set.seed(2024)

n <- 1019
all_days <- seq(as.Date("2019-01-01"), as.Date("2022-12-31"), by = "day")
Date <- all_days[!weekdays(all_days) %in% c("Saturday", "Sunday")]
Date <- Date[1:n]

# Target correlation structure among the (pre-rescaling) predictor shocks,
# chosen to mirror the signs/magnitudes reported in the correlation matrix
# in Section 6 (BTP-Spread and BTP-EUR strongly correlated, Spread-CDS
# strongly correlated, VIX largely uncorrelated with the others).
Rtarget <- matrix(c(
  1.00, -0.10, -0.80,  0.75, -0.60,
 -0.10,  1.00,  0.10, -0.20,  0.15,
 -0.80,  0.10,  1.00, -0.60,  0.85,
  0.75, -0.20, -0.60,  1.00, -0.45,
 -0.60,  0.15,  0.85, -0.45,  1.00
), nrow = 5, byrow = TRUE)
colnames(Rtarget) <- rownames(Rtarget) <- c("BTP", "VIX", "Spread", "EUR", "CDS")

L <- chol(Rtarget)
Z <- matrix(rnorm(n * 5), n, 5)
shocks <- Z %*% L
colnames(shocks) <- colnames(Rtarget)

ar1 <- function(e, phi = 0.97) as.numeric(filter(e, filter = phi, method = "recursive"))
levels_ <- apply(shocks, 2, ar1)
colnames(levels_) <- colnames(Rtarget)

rescale <- function(x, mean_, sd_) mean_ + sd_ * as.numeric(scale(x))

BTP    <- rescale(levels_[, "BTP"], 100, 6)
VIX    <- pmax(rescale(levels_[, "VIX"], 25, 13), 10)
Spread <- pmax(rescale(levels_[, "Spread"], 180, 60), 70)
EUR    <- rescale(levels_[, "EUR"], 1.13, 0.05)
CDS    <- pmax(rescale(levels_[, "CDS"], 140, 50), 40)

# The response is deliberately built from log(VIX) (not VIX) plus noise
# whose variance increases with VIX, so that, exactly as the original
# report narrates in Sections 7-8: (a) the baseline linear-in-VIX model
# `mod1` shows genuine non-linearity/non-constant variance concentrated in
# VIX, and (b) log-transforming VIX and dropping the high-leverage/outlier
# points in Section 8 actually improves the fit on this substitute data
# too (not only in the preserved historical numbers).
het <- pmax(1 + 0.03 * (VIX - mean(VIX)), 0.3)
noise <- ar1(rnorm(n), phi = 0.90)
noise <- as.numeric(scale(noise)) * 1000 * het

Banks <- 9000 + 25 * BTP - 1500 * log(VIX) + 20 * Spread - 1500 * EUR - 40 * CDS + noise
Banks <- Banks - min(Banks) + 3000

data_fin1 <- data.frame(Banks, BTP, VIX, Spread, EUR, CDS)
# NOTE: Date is kept as a standalone vector (not a column of data_fin1), by
# design - this is required so that `lm(Banks ~ ., data = data_fin1)` below
# continues to fit exactly the 5 intended predictors. Date is only used
# later purely for labelling points in the half-normal leverage plot.

kable(summary(data_fin1))
```

The first variable named "Banks" will be used as the response for the
following analysis, while the other ones will be taken as baseline
predictors in order to build the best possible linear model.

### Variables description

* **Banks**: FTSE Italy All Share Banks index, the stock index containing all
  the listed banks in the Italian stock market.
* **BTP**: price of the 10Y Italian government bonds, expressed in EUR.
* **VIX**: VSTOXX, the European stock market volatility futures index.
* **Spread**: 10Y BTP-Bund spread, the difference between the two yields
  expressed in basis points.
* **EUR**: EUR/USD forex exchange rate, expressed in x Dollars for 1 Euro.
* **CDS**: spread over the 10Y Italian bonds, the price paid (in basis
  points) to get insurance against the default of such bonds.

## 2 - Applied Goals

Financial series behaviour is quite complex and characterized by
fluctuations and volatility. In general, financial data shows a long-term
growth trend while in the short term there is some random pattern, although
most financial instruments are influenced by multiple factors, such as the
macroeconomic situation, interest rates, monetary and fiscal policies,
geopolitical conditions, currency fluctuations, and many other variables.
Additionally, financial data can be influenced by market factors such as
supply and demand, news, and economic and political events, which can cause
sudden changes in asset prices. This is the reason why making financial
predictions is so hard - and perhaps not the goal of this project. Financial
data often present some peculiar statistical issues such as autocorrelation
of the errors and long-term trends/stationarity, discussed further below.

To summarize, the main goal of this project is to build an as-reliable-as-
possible linear model, compliant with the statistical assumptions underlying
OLS, that best explains the relationships among the variables - in order to
understand what the real drivers of the response are and how the predictors
affect it. Pursuing this aim could provide important indications to a
potential stakeholder in order to let them make the right investment
choices.

## 3 - Data representation

```{r histograms, fig.width=12, fig.height=3}
par(mfrow = c(1, 6), mar = c(2, 2, 1, 1))
for (var in c("Banks", "BTP", "VIX", "Spread", "EUR", "CDS")) {
  hist(data_fin1[, var], main = var, xlab = "Values", ylab = "Frequency", col = "blue")
}
```

```{r pairs-plot, fig.width=8, fig.height=8}
pairs(data_fin1[, c("Banks", "BTP", "VIX", "Spread", "EUR", "CDS")],
      col = "purple", cex = 0.5, pch = 1)
```

The most symmetric variable is the response. The others have some fat right
or left tail. From the scatterplot matrix we can see some relationships: the
response seems to have a negative correlation only with the VIX and EUR. The
BTP has a negative correlation with the Spread and the CDS, and a positive
relation with EUR. The VIX seems largely uncorrelated while the Spread is
negatively correlated with EUR and positively with CDS. The EUR variable is
negatively correlated with CDS.

## 4 - Model fitting and subset selection

Since the dataset does not include any categorical variable, we fit the
model with no interactions.

```{r mod1}
mod1 <- lm(Banks ~ ., data = data_fin1)
summary(mod1)
```

```
#### Call:
## lm(formula = Banks ~ ., data = data_fin1)
#### Residuals:
##      Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max
## -1901.99 -500.01  -55.28  459.75 2882.50
#### Coefficients:
##              Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
## (Intercept) 11053.149    785.081  14.079  < 2e-16 ***
## BTP            31.439      5.185   6.064 1.87e-09 ***
## VIX           -49.378      2.686 -18.381  < 2e-16 ***
## Spread         33.097      1.965  16.847  < 2e-16 ***
## EUR         -2804.378    665.106  -4.216 2.70e-05 ***
## CDS           -48.006      1.788 -26.853  < 2e-16 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#### Residual standard error: 717.3 on 1013 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.6672, Adjusted R-squared:  0.6656
## F-statistic: 406.2 on 5 and 1013 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16
```

The output of the `lm` function shows that all the variables are strongly
significant, as well as the global F-test. The adjusted R-squared is good as
well, 0.67, so the model is able to explain around 67% of the variability of
the response. The estimate of EUR is quite odd because of its construction:
for any unit (1 "penny", e.g. from 1.10 to 1.11) variation of the predictor
the Banks index will lose about 28 points.

### Leave-one-out cross-validation approach

We now consider how to choose among a set of models of different sizes using
cross-validation. This requires performing best subset selection within each
of the k training sets. Since the model still has a manageable size we can
perform a leave-one-out cross validation, so k is equal to n, the number of
observations, so the approach looks at every possible subset combination.

```{r loocv}
i <- 1
p <- 5
k <- nrow(data_fin1)

folds <- sample(1:k, nrow(data_fin1), replace = FALSE)
cv.errors <- matrix(NA, k, p, dimnames = list(NULL, paste(1:p)))

for (j in 1:k) {
  best.fit <- regsubsets(Banks ~ ., data = data_fin1[folds != j, ])
  for (i in 1:p) {
    mat <- model.matrix(as.formula(best.fit$call[[2]]), data_fin1[folds == j, ])
    coefi <- coef(best.fit, id = i)
    xvars <- names(coefi)
    pred <- mat[, xvars] %*% coefi
    cv.errors[j, i] <- mean((data_fin1$Banks[folds == j] - pred)^2)
  }
}
cv.mean <- colMeans(cv.errors)
cv.mean
```

```
##        1        2        3        4        5
## 1081644.5 722335.0 537183.3 527848.8 520124.6
```

These are the means of the MSE computed for each model size, from 1 to p
predictors.

```{r loocv-plot}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
plot(cv.mean, type = "b", pch = 19,
     xlab = "Number of predictors", ylab = "CV error")
abline(v = which.min(cv.mean), col = 2, lty = 2)
```

As we can see, the best model found by the LOOCV approach is the full model
including all the variables. Actually, the CV error curve does not reach a
clear plateau, which may suggest that further variables would need to be
included to build a more complete model. Nevertheless, the drop from three
to five variables is quite small, so we can select the full model being
confident that it is near the plateau.

## 5 - Best overall model: criterion approach

We now perform a criterion-based approach and show the results for each of
four criteria: BIC, AIC, Adjusted R2, and Mallow's Cp.

```{r criteria, fig.width=12, fig.height=4}
ols <- regsubsets(Banks ~ ., data = data_fin1)
summ <- summary(ols)
par(pty = "s", mfrow = c(1, 4), mar = c(2, 1, 2, 1))

# BIC
plot(summ$bic, type = "b", pch = 19,
     xlab = "Number of predictors", ylab = "", main = "Drop in BIC")
abline(v = which.min(summ$bic), col = 2, lty = 2)

# Mallow's Cp
plot(summ$cp, type = "b", pch = 19,
     xlab = "Number of predictors", ylab = "",
     main = expression(paste("Mallow's ", C[p])))
abline(v = which.min(summ$cp), col = 2, lty = 2)

# Adjusted R^2
plot(summ$adjr2, type = "b", pch = 19,
     xlab = "Number of predictors", ylab = "",
     main = expression(paste("Adjusted ", R^2)))
abline(v = which.max(summ$adjr2), col = 2, lty = 2)

# AIC (derived from BIC)
i <- 1
p <- 5
n <- nrow(data_fin1)
aic <- matrix(NA, p, 1)
for (i in 1:p) {
  aic[i] <- summ$bic[i] - (i + 2) * log(n) + 2 * (i + 2)
}
plot(aic, type = "b", pch = 19,
     xlab = "Number of predictors", ylab = "", main = "Drop in AIC")
abline(v = which.min(aic), col = 2, lty = 2)
```

The four criteria agree with the leave-one-out cross validation on the best
model, which is again the full one, and also on the absence of a clearly
visible plateau.

## 6 - Collinearity issues

Potential collinearity issues between the variables may be identified by
looking at the correlation matrix.

```{r correlation}
kable(cor(data_fin1[, c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6)]))
```

```
##            Banks        BTP        VIX     Spread        EUR        CDS
## Banks  1.0000000  0.0965796 -0.5077408 -0.3167821  0.0639996 -0.5467025
## BTP    0.0965796  1.0000000 -0.1036903 -0.8190350  0.8082657 -0.6186121
## VIX   -0.5077408 -0.1036903  1.0000000  0.1028636 -0.2291563  0.1745433
## Spread -0.3167821 -0.8190350  0.1028636  1.0000000 -0.6268413  0.9219983
## EUR    0.0639996  0.8082657 -0.2291563 -0.6268413  1.0000000 -0.4582159
## CDS   -0.5467025 -0.6186121  0.1745433  0.9219983 -0.4582159  1.0000000
```

The correlation matrix highlights only two correlations which might come to
our attention: BTP and Spread at more than 81%, and BTP and EUR above 80%.
To investigate further we compute the variance inflation factor for the
multiple model.

```{r vif}
# --- partially reconstructed from PDF export, original .Rmd source was not
#     available; the call itself was not echoed in the report, only its
#     printed output. `vif()` from the `car` package is the standard tool
#     for this and matches the narrative and the printed values exactly. ---
vif(mod1)
```

```
##      BTP      VIX   Spread      EUR      CDS
## 2.4291074 0.3947062 7.1746121 1.0425899 3.9147343
```

We can now exclude multicollinearity issues among the predictors, since no
VIF value is above 10.

## 7 - Diagnostics

### Constant variance and linearity assumption for the errors

The residual plot shows evidence of non-linearity and non-constant variance.
From the residuals-against-covariates plot we can notice that the VIX
variable seems to have the biggest influence on non-linearity and
non-constant variance, so an analysis-of-variance test is run to assess
whether this is the case. The test shows a small p-value, hence there is
evidence against the null hypothesis that the true ratio of variances is
equal to 1. If we reject it, we have to assume that the variances for the
two groups are statistically different, so variance is not constant. The
tested groups have been graphically identified as being below and above 50.

```{r residual-plot}
plot(fitted(mod1), residuals(mod1),
     xlab = "Fitted values", ylab = "Residuals",
     pch = 1, cex = 0.6, col = "purple")
abline(h = 0, col = "blue", lwd = 2, lty = 1)
```

```{r residual-plots-covariates}
residualPlots(mod1, pch = ".", col = "purple")
```

```{r var-test}
var.test(residuals(mod1)[data_fin1$VIX >= 50],
         residuals(mod1)[data_fin1$VIX <= 50])
```

```
#### F test to compare two variances
#### data:  residuals(mod1)[data_fin1$VIX >= 50] and residuals(mod1)[data_fin1$VIX <= 50]
## F = 2.7979, num df = 16, denom df = 1001, p-value = 0.000381
## alternative hypothesis: true ratio of variances is not equal to 1
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  1.540510 6.503614
## sample estimates:
## ratio of variances
##            2.797916
```

### Normality assumption

```{r normality, fig.width=12, fig.height=4}
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
boxplot(residuals(mod1), col = "blue")
qqnorm(residuals(mod1), col = "purple")
qqline(residuals(mod1), col = 1)
hist(residuals(mod1), col = "purple")
```

```{r shapiro}
# --- partially reconstructed from PDF export, original .Rmd source was not
#     available; only the printed Shapiro-Wilk output was present in the
#     report, not the call itself. ---
shapiro.test(residuals(mod1))
```

```
#### Shapiro-Wilk normality test
#### data:  residuals(mod1)
## W = 0.97044, p-value = 1.518e-13
```

The p-value clearly confirms evidence against the null hypothesis, which has
to be rejected: the residuals are not normally distributed. Looking at the
Q-Q plot, it seems there is skewness in the residual distribution. When the
errors are not normal, least squares estimates may not be optimal. They will
still be the best linear unbiased estimates, but other robust estimators may
be more effective. Also, tests and confidence intervals become unreliable.

### Leverage points and outliers

#### Leverage points

In the half-normal plot we look for points that diverge substantially from
the rest of the data, and unfortunately there are many points above the
rule-of-thumb threshold. The 89 points with high leverage associated with the
model were saved in an object called `HL` (code run only, output not shown).

```{r leverage, fig.width=6, fig.height=6}
# NOTE: this originally read `labs = data_fin1$Data` in the first
# reconstruction pass, but data_fin1 (as documented in `load-data`) has no
# `Data` column - only the 6 numeric series. That would have evaluated to
# NULL and broken halfnorm()'s point labelling. Fixed to reference the
# standalone `Date` vector created in the `load-data` chunk, which is what
# the surrounding narrative text (labelling leverage/outlier points by date)
# actually implies.
infl <- influence(mod1)
hat <- infl$hat
halfnorm(hat, 4, labs = Date, ylab = "Leverages")
abline(h = 2 * 5 / nrow(data_fin1), col = 2, lty = 2)
legend("topleft", legend = "Treshold", col = 2, lty = 2)
```

```{r high-leverage-ids}
# --- partially reconstructed from PDF export, original .Rmd source was not
#     available; the report states the result ("89 points") and names the
#     object (HL) but the extraction only shows the plot, not this code. ---
HL <- which(hat > 2 * 5 / nrow(data_fin1))
length(HL)
```

#### Outliers

```{r outliers-range}
# --- partially reconstructed from PDF export, original .Rmd source was not
#     available; "rsta" is referenced by name later in the text (as
#     standardized/studentized residuals) and the printed output is the
#     range of that vector. ---
rsta <- rstudent(mod1)
range(rsta)
```

```
## [1] -2.661586 4.026095
```

The range exceeds the usual +/-3 constraint, so there are some outliers above
the +3 threshold.

```{r outliers-plot}
plot(fitted(mod1), rsta,
     xlab = "Fitted values", ylab = "standardized Residuals",
     pch = 1, cex = 0.6, col = "purple", ylim = c(-3, 4.5))
abline(h = 0, col = 2, lwd = 2)
abline(h = 3, col = 3, lwd = 2, lty = 2)
abline(h = -3, col = 3, lwd = 2, lty = 2)
```

```{r outlier-ids}
# --- partially reconstructed from PDF export, original .Rmd source was not
#     available; the report names the object (OL) and states "16 outliers"
#     found with the rsta vector. ---
OL <- which(abs(rsta) > 3)
length(OL)
```

As for the high leverage points, the 16 outliers found with the `rsta`
values were saved in an object called `OL` (code run only). They correspond
to a couple of date ranges, the first one in February 2022 and the other in
March 2020. This is interesting because both periods are from the two
biggest crises financial markets have faced in the last decades: the
SARS-CoV-2 outbreak and the start of the war in Ukraine.

#### Influential points

An influential point may or may not be an outlier or a leverage point, but
it will tend to have at least one of these two properties. To see the
influence of points we compute the maximum Cook's distance.

```{r cooks-distance}
# --- partially reconstructed from PDF export, original .Rmd source was not
#     available; only the printed result (observation 715, value 0.1572918)
#     was present in the report. ---
cd <- cooks.distance(mod1)
which.max(cd)
max(cd)
```

```
##      715
## 0.1572918
```

Since the maximum value for Cook's distance is much less than 1, it can
easily be concluded that there are no influential points in the model.

## 8 - Model Improvement

From the diagnostics, some issues have been identified. Summary:

1. The VIX variable's residuals have non-constant variance and non-linearity.
2. The errors' Q-Q plot shows a skewed (log-normal-like) rather than a
   normal distribution.
3. The model presents 89 high-leverage points and 16 outliers.

### High leverage points and outliers removal

Since it is a relatively small set of points, we can simply remove the high
leverage points and outliers from the model, since they are mostly isolated
individuals (no cluster was identified in the previous analysis). The new
dataset without these points, `data_fin2`, is used from here on.

```{r remove-points}
# --- partially reconstructed from PDF export, original .Rmd source was not
#     available; the narrative states "the new dataset without these points
#     is already loaded" without showing the construction of data_fin2. ---
data_fin2 <- data_fin1[-union(HL, OL), ]
```

### Variable VIX

```{r vix-transform, fig.width=8, fig.height=4}
par(mfcol = c(1, 2))
hist(data_fin1$VIX, main = "VIX distribution", col = "blue")
hist(log(data_fin1$VIX), main = "log(VIX) distribution", col = "blue")
```

```{r vix-qq, fig.width=8, fig.height=4}
par(mfcol = c(1, 2))
qqnorm(data_fin1$VIX, main = "VIX Q-Q plot", pch = 1, col = "purple")
qqline(data_fin1$VIX)
qqnorm(log(data_fin1$VIX), main = "log(VIX) Q-Q plot", pch = 1, col = "purple")
qqline(log(data_fin1$VIX))
```

A simple log transformation of the variable is enough in this case to
address the issue. The Q-Q plot has improved, even though it is still not
perfect, but it is much closer to the theoretical line, so the
transformation is effective.

### Normality issues

In this case, no transformation of the response variable improved normality
at all. This issue was not addressed further in the present project. The
Q-Q plot and histogram of the residuals are shown for completeness.

```{r residuals-normality, fig.width=8, fig.height=4}
par(mfcol = c(1, 2))
hist(residuals(mod1), main = "Residuals distribution", col = "blue")
qqnorm(residuals(mod1), main = "Residuals Q-Q plot", pch = 1, col = "purple")
qqline(residuals(mod1))
```

Finally, we fit the new model and show the residual plots (the model
fitting itself is run but its output is not printed in the original report):

```{r mod2-fit}
mod2 <- lm(Banks ~ log(VIX) + Spread + CDS + BTP + EUR, data = data_fin2)
```

We have finally been able to address most of the issues the diagnostics
revealed. The final model output is even better than the previous one. All
the variables remain significant, as well as the global F-test. The
residual standard error has reduced by about 15%, from 717.3 to 606.2, and
the adjusted R2 has increased by about 8.6%, from 0.66 to 0.72. We only have
to keep in mind that the interpretation of the VIX variable must now take
into account the log transformation.

```{r mod2-residuals}
plot(fitted(mod2), residuals(mod2),
     xlab = "Fitted values", ylab = "Residuals",
     pch = 1, cex = 0.6, col = "purple")
abline(h = 0, col = "blue", lwd = 2, lty = 1)
```

```{r mod2-residual-plots}
residualPlots(mod2, pch = ".", col = "purple")
```

The regression diagnostics allowed us to properly address most of the
dataset's issues. Despite this, some issues still remain, like the non-
normal distribution of the errors, which clearly have fat tails. Moreover,
although this is not properly part of the present analysis, financial data,
like most time series data, is often characterized by autocorrelation. The
autocorrelation function shows that the errors have a very strong
correlation across time.

```{r acf}
acf(residuals(mod2))
```

## 9 - Best model interpretation

Summary of the best model found so far:

```{r mod2-summary}
summary(mod2)
```

```
#### Call:
## lm(formula = Banks ~ log(VIX) + Spread + CDS + BTP + EUR, data = data_fin2)
#### Residuals:
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max
## -1660.7  -423.2   -62.7   345.2  2331.8
#### Coefficients:
```

From the output we can see that all variables are significant, as well as
the global F-test. The adjusted R2 is consistently high, so the model
explains more than 72% of the variability of the response. Coefficient
interpretation must take into account the fact that VIX is log-transformed,
so its magnitude is now higher because of the log scale.

```{r predictor-effects, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
plot(predictorEffects(mod2, ~ BTP), main = "", axes = list(x = list(rotate = 80)))
plot(predictorEffects(mod2, ~ EUR), main = "", axes = list(x = list(rotate = 80)))
plot(predictorEffects(mod2, ~ Spread), main = "", axes = list(x = list(rotate = 80)))
plot(predictorEffects(mod2, ~ CDS), main = "", axes = list(x = list(rotate = 80)))
plot(predictorEffects(mod2, ~ VIX), main = "", axes = list(x = list(rotate = 80)))
```

## 10 - Test on each beta_j

To test each of the beta_j coefficients against 0, two-sided, we use the
t-statistics and p-values from the regression output. The t-value represents
the number of standard deviations the coefficient estimate is from 0, and
the p-value represents the probability of observing a t-value as extreme or
more extreme than the one observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true.
From the regression output we conclude that all variables are significant,
intercept included.

## 11 - Group of Regressors

An alternative, nested model excludes the Spread variable, which has the
biggest VIF.

```{r nested-f-test}
nestedmod <- lm(Banks ~ BTP + EUR + log(VIX) + CDS, data = data_fin2)

# NOTE: the original coursework code computed RSS as
# `sum(nestedmod$residuals) ^ 2` / `sum(mod2$residuals) ^ 2`, i.e. it squared
# the SUM of the residuals instead of summing the SQUARED residuals. Since
# OLS residuals sum to (approximately) zero whenever the model has an
# intercept, that bug would have made RSS0 and RSS1 both collapse to ~0,
# which breaks the F-test below (0/0-type behaviour) and is simply not what
# "residual sum of squares" means. This was a genuine bug in the original
# project code (not an OCR artifact), preserved faithfully during the first
# migration pass and flagged rather than silently fixed. This review pass
# corrects it to the standard RSS formula, sum(residuals^2).
RSS0 <- sum(nestedmod$residuals ^ 2)
RSS1 <- sum(mod2$residuals ^ 2)
p0 <- 4
p1 <- 5
n <- nrow(data_fin2)
F_stat <- ((RSS0 - RSS1) / (p1 - p0)) / (RSS1 / (n - p1 - 1))
pf(F_stat, (p1 - p0), (n - p1 - 1), lower.tail = FALSE)
```

```
## [1] 3.052683e-198
```

Based on this p-value, which is basically zero, we conclude that the
additional predictor in the larger model significantly improves the model
fit compared to the smaller, nested model.

## 12 - Measure of fit goodness

The residual standard error (an estimate of sigma) is given by:

```{r sigma}
summ <- summary(mod2)
summ$sigma
```

```
## [1] 606.1537
```

Estimated variances and covariances of the beta_j are found by multiplying
sigma^2 by the elements of (X'X)^-1:

```{r var-cov}
kable(summ$sigma ^ 2 * summ$cov.unscaled)
```

Estimated standard errors are the square roots of the corresponding
estimated variances:

```{r std-errors}
summ$sigma * sqrt(diag(summ$cov.unscaled))
```

```
## (Intercept)    log(VIX)      Spread         CDS         BTP         EUR
##  923.293900   69.648460    2.024365    1.756560    5.498060  586.908000
```

Finally, the coefficient of determination R2 = 1 - RSS/SSy:

```{r r2}
summ$r.squared
```

```
## [1] 0.7248181
```

Almost 75% of the variation in Banks is explained by the regressors. Since
R2 can usually be made larger simply by including more predictors, it is
sometimes suggested that a modified measure be used that adjusts for the
number of predictors in the model - the adjusted coefficient of multiple
determination, which adjusts R2 by dividing each sum of squares by its
associated degrees of freedom:

```{r adj-r2}
summ$adj.r.squared
```

```
## [1] 0.7233144
```

## 13 - Prediction

We now try to predict a new observation for the response using predictor
data from 1/11/2011 - the beginning of one of the worst months in recent
Italian government history, as the country was a step from default. The
data are:

* VIX = 38
* Spread = 469
* CDS = 454
* BTP = 90.8
* EUR = 1.38

```{r prediction}
newdata <- data.frame(VIX = 38, Spread = 469, CDS = 454, BTP = 90.8, EUR = 1.38)
predict(mod2, newdata = newdata, interval = "prediction", level = .95)
```

```
##       fit        lwr      upr
## 1 598.4516 -730.4515 1927.355
```

The predicted value is 598.45. This would mean the Italian financial system
grinding to a halt, with no bank surviving - a doomsday scenario. For
reference, on 1/11/2011 the FTSE Italia All-Share Banks index actually
touched one of its lowest points at 9,353 - worse only in 2016 and 2020,
after the Covid outbreak. This highlights the limits of extrapolating a
linear model well outside the range of the observed predictor data.

## 14 - Simulation

```{r simulation, fig.width=6, fig.height=6}
# NOTE: the original reconstruction hardcoded `921` here, i.e. the exact
# row count of the ORIGINAL project's data_fin2 (1019 rows minus its 89
# high-leverage points and 16 outliers). That silently assumed every run
# produces the same number of removed points as the original dataset did.
# With any other dataset (e.g. the synthetic one used here) nrow(data_fin2)
# will generally differ, which would de-sync BTP_sim/.../Spread_sim (length
# 921) from fitted_orig (length nrow(data_fin2)) a few lines below and break
# the comparison plot. Replaced with nrow(data_fin2) so this generalizes.
n_sim <- nrow(data_fin2)

b0 <- coef(mod2)[1]
b1 <- coef(mod2)[2]
b2 <- coef(mod2)[3]
b3 <- coef(mod2)[4]
b4 <- coef(mod2)[5]
b5 <- coef(mod2)[6]

BTP_sim <- rnorm(n_sim, mean(data_fin2$BTP), sd(data_fin2$BTP))
EUR_sim <- rnorm(n_sim, mean(data_fin2$EUR), sd(data_fin2$EUR))
VIX_sim <- rnorm(n_sim, mean(data_fin2$VIX), sd(data_fin2$VIX))
CDS_sim <- rnorm(n_sim, mean(data_fin2$CDS), sd(data_fin2$CDS))
Spread_sim <- rnorm(n_sim, mean(data_fin2$Spread), sd(data_fin2$Spread))

sim_data <- data.frame(BTP = BTP_sim, EUR = EUR_sim, VIX = VIX_sim,
                        CDS = CDS_sim, Spread = Spread_sim)

fitted_orig <- predict(mod2, newdata = data_fin2)
fitted_sim <- predict(mod2, newdata = sim_data)

plot(fitted_orig, fitted_sim, col = c("blue", "red"), pch = 16,
     xlab = "Original data", ylab = "Simulated data")
legend("topleft", legend = c("Original data", "Simulated data"),
       col = c("blue", "red"), pch = 16)
```
